newsitem.title: UK: POLL-Sleaze factor refuses to go away--Reuters poll.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Sleaze factor refuses to go away--Reuters poll.

text.p: Nearly half of the British electorate believe the sex and financial scandals which held centre stage in the first weeks of the British election campaign will affect the final outcome, a Reuters/NOP poll published on Monday showed.
The exclusive poll showed that 43 percent of the respondents thought the sagas of sleaze which have smeared the ruling Conservative Party will affect the final results "a lot" or "a little".
The Conservative Party is already well behind in the polls, with the Reuters/NOP survey on Monday indicating a 21-point lead for the main opposition Labour Party among those who had made a decision.

Although seven out of 10 respondents in the poll said the scandals would make no difference to their own personal voting decisions, analysts said the negative influence on the Conservatives was bound to trickle through.
They said the 14 percent who thought they would be influenced a lot or a little by the allegations were the undecided floating voters both major parties were determined to woo.
"This must have some kind of effect on the floating voter," said Colin Rallings, reader in politics at the University of Plymouth.
"Committed voters are not going to change their mind, their loyalties are clear no matter what. But those who are undecided are going to remember this," he said.
The scandals which have dogged the Conservatives' election campaign are hard for the voter to forget.
MPs have been faced with a ruthless publicity spotlight on their private lives, forcing some potential parliamentary hopefuls to step down and others to fight for their political lives.

The Conservatives have suffered a new blow to their re-election hopes in the shape of a veteran BBC reporter who has stepped forward to stand as an "anti-sleaze" candidate against a former government minister accused of corruption.
Both main opposition parties have backed BBC war correspondent Martin Bell, one of Britain's best-known journalists, to stand against former minister Neil Hamilton in the May 1 election.

Hamilton, who denies receiving cash for asking parliamentary questions, has come under pressure from his party leadership to quit but local Conservatives in his Tatton constituency in northwest England have stood by him.
The debate over public and private morality waned somewhat last week after one married MP succeeded in gaining the support of local backers despite being seen kissing a nightclub hostess.
But the Reuters/NOP poll showed that the nightmare was not yet over for the beleaguered Conservatives.

"It is a relatively small number of people saying sleaze will make a difference to their personal vote. But these are probably marginal voters and every percentage at the margin is crucial," said Dominic Wring, of Nottingham Trent University.
